html:
Cato the Elder was a Roman soldier, statesman and writer who lived from 234 to 149 BCE. He stood for old Roman values of hard work, thrift and duty, and fought against Greek luxury and fashions.

He was a "new man" from Tusculum, the first of his family to reach the Senate. He fought in the Second Punic War, and as consul in 195 BCE he spoke against repealing the Lex Oppia, a law limiting women's luxury, and lost. As censor in 184 BCE he was famously strict: he put heavy taxes on luxury goods and expelled senators he judged unworthy. He also hounded his rival Scipio Africanus in the courts.

He was the first major writer of Latin prose. His Origines was the first history of Rome in Latin, and his book on farming (On Agriculture) is the oldest Latin prose work to survive whole.

In old age he ended his speeches by saying that Carthage must be destroyed. He died in 149 BCE, as that war began; Carthage fell in 146 BCE (Rome destroys Carthage and Corinth). His great grandson was Cato the Younger.
